title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

reading.body:
This is a false positive from an automated sensor that was acted on as though it were an identification. A license plate reader misread a single character and produced a match to a stolen vehicle, and the enforcement step that followed treated that match as sufficient grounds. The failure sits at the handoff between the alert and the officer's response, not in the camera alone.

Catching it would have required verifying the alert independently before enforcement, which is what the vendor itself says should happen. A one-character discrepancy is the kind of thing a comparison against the plate or the vehicle description would surface. Nothing in the account indicates that check occurred.

What is not established is the cause. The claim that a tinted plate cover produced the misread comes from the sheriff's office, and the same office concluded the deputy's actions were reasonable. Those are the agency's accounts, not independent findings, and no court has ruled on the detention.

reports.title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

summary: Steven Melvin, a 42-year-old motorist in York County, South Carolina, was reportedly detained at gunpoint for more than five minutes. A Flock Safety automated license plate reader misread the first letter of his plate and matched his BMW to a similar stolen vehicle. The sheriff’s office later said an illegal tinted plate cover caused the malfunction and found the deputy’s actions reasonable. Flock said alerts should be independently verified before enforcement.
